Here are several proven strategies that an apartment building can pursue to bring down its collective heating costs. Many of these measures also improve comfort and can raise the building’s EPC energy class:

1. Optimize the Building Envelope  
  • Add or upgrade insulation in external walls, roof and—if applicable—under the ground floor slab.  
  • Install high-performance, triple- or double-glazed windows with low-emissivity coatings.  
  • Seal air leaks around windows, doors, electrical penetrations and service shafts to improve airtightness.

2. Upgrade the Heating System  
  • Replace old boilers with a modern, high-efficiency condensing boiler (if gas- or oil-fired).  
  • Consider installing a ground- or air-source heat pump, which can cut heating energy use by 30–50 %.  
  • Where district heating is available, negotiate lower tariffs or switch to a more efficient supplier.

3. Improve Distribution and Controls  
  • Fit thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) on all radiators so residents can control individual room temperatures.  
  • Install a smart or weather-compensating central control system that adjusts flow temperature to outdoor conditions.  
  • Balance the system so that each stairwell or apartment receives the correct flow of hot water.

4. Ventilation with Heat Recovery  
  • Switch to a mechanical ventilation system equipped with a heat-recovery unit (MVHR). This recovers up to 90 % of the heat from outgoing air.  
  • Ensure filters are regularly cleaned and the system is properly maintained to preserve performance.

5. Renewable and Supplemental Energy  
  • Install solar-thermal collectors on the roof to pre-heat domestic hot water or supplement space heating.  
  • Integrate photovoltaic (PV) panels and consider battery storage; surplus electricity can run heat pumps.  
  • Explore biomass boilers if local biomass resources and fuel logistics make sense for your region.

6. Resident Engagement and Monitoring  
  • Fit individual heat meters in each apartment. Billing based on actual use incentivizes residents to be more energy-conscious.  
  • Provide clear guidance on optimal indoor temperatures (e.g., 20 – 21 °C living rooms, 16 – 18 °C bedrooms).  
  • Use an energy-monitoring dashboard in the common areas or online portal to show collective savings and encourage further efforts.

7. Use the EPC as a Roadmap  
  • Review your latest EPC (“epc_egienergiklass”) to identify recommended measures and their estimated payback times.  
  • Focus first on “low-hanging fruit” measures with short payback (e.g., sealing drafts, radiator valves) before moving on to major investments (e.g., façade insulation).

By combining airtightness improvements, system upgrades, intelligent controls and resident engagement, an apartment building can typically reduce its heating consumption by 20 – 40 %—often recouping the investment within 5–10 years.

An energy declaration (in Sweden often called an energideklaration or EPC) is primarily intended to give a building’s board or management clear, standardized information about the building’s current energy performance and opportunities for improvement.  In practice it will typically include:

1. Energy class (epc_egienergiklass)  
   • A letter grade (A–G) that ranks the building’s overall energy efficiency.  
   • If more than one declaration exists, the most recent rating is the one to rely on.  

2. Actual and normalized energy use  
   • Measured energy consumption per square meter of heated floor area (A-temp).  
   • Breakdown by energy carrier (electricity, district heating, oil, etc.).  

3. Building characteristics  
   • Type of building (epc_egenbyggnadstyp) – e.g. detached house, apartment block, commercial premises.  
   • Heated floor area (epc_egenatemp) and number of above-ground floors (epc_egenantalplan).  
   • Number of stairwells/trapphus (epc_egenantaltrapphus), which can affect common-area heating requirements.  
   • Whether the building was owner-built (epc_egennybyggar).  

4. Technical systems and insulation  
   • Description of heating, ventilation and cooling installations.  
   • Information on insulation levels in walls, roof and windows.  

5. Recommended energy‐saving measures  
   • A prioritized list of upgrades (e.g. improved insulation, window replacement, heat‐pump installation).  
   • Estimated investment costs, energy savings and payback times for each measure.  

6. Compliance and reporting data  
   • EPC reference numbers (byggnadsid, 50a_uuid, epc_idadr) for traceability.  
   • Confirmation that the declaration meets national regulatory requirements.  

For a building board, the declaration is both a compliance document and a decision‐support tool. It provides a snapshot of current energy performance, highlights potential cost‐saving upgrades, and helps prioritize long‐term renovation or maintenance plans.

To reduce your building’s heating costs most effectively, you should focus on improving its overall energy performance—ideally as measured by the EPC energy class (epc_egienergiklass). In practice, the key priorities are:  

1.  Upgrade the building envelope  
    •  Roof insulation: Because heat always rises, upgrading or adding insulation in the attic or roof space typically offers the highest return on investment.  
    •  Wall insulation: For uninsulated or poorly insulated walls, consider cavity‐fill insulation or an external/internal insulation system.  
    •  Floor insulation: Insulating over unheated basements or crawl spaces stops cold bridging from below.  

2.  Improve window and door performance  
    •  Install high‐performance, double‐ or triple‐glazed windows with low-emissivity coatings.  
    •  Ensure doors and windows are properly sealed with weather-stripping to reduce drafts and infiltration.  

3.  Enhance airtightness  
    •  Locate and seal leaks around service penetrations, junctions, and transitions (e.g. between wall and floor or around window frames).  
    •  Conduct a blower-door test to identify and systematically eliminate air leaks.  

4.  Optimize mechanical systems  
    •  Heat recovery ventilation (HRV): A balanced ventilation system with heat recovery will supply fresh air while recapturing heat from outgoing stale air.  
    •  High‐efficiency heating source: Consider replacing an old boiler with a modern condensing boiler or a ground/air-source heat pump.  
    •  Smart controls and thermostatic radiators: Zoning and programmable thermostats let you heat only occupied areas when needed.  

5.  Review heated floor area (Atemp) and usage patterns  
    •  epc_egenatemp tells you the total heated volume—if certain wings or floors are little used, consider zoning them off or reducing their setpoint.  
    •  Adjust thermostat setbacks for nights and unoccupied periods to cut wasted energy.  

6.  Seek an updated EPC assessment  
    •  A new energy performance certificate will quantify the impact of any measures you’ve taken and guide you toward the next most cost-effective upgrade.  

By tackling the building envelope first (insulation, airtightness, windows) and then optimizing ventilation and heating systems, you’ll achieve the greatest reduction in heating costs per krona invested—and most likely improve your EPC energy class in the process.

Direct‐acting electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the incoming electrical energy into heat at the point of use – so in that very limited sense they’re “efficient” (no heat is lost through ducting or flue gases). However, when we look at the bigger picture of energy efficiency and running cost, there are two important considerations:  

1. Primary‐energy efficiency and carbon footprint  
   • Electricity generation is seldom 100 percent efficient – losses occur in generation, transmission and distribution.   
   • If your grid mix includes coal or gas, each kilowatt‐hour you pay for will have already required more than one kilowatt‐hour of primary energy to produce.  

2. Operating cost compared to alternatives  
   • Electricity is generally more expensive per kWh than district heating, natural gas or oil, so your heating bill will be higher in most markets.  
   • Modern heat pumps can deliver 3–4 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity consumed (COP 3–4), making them 200–300 percent more “energy‐efficient” in use than direct‐acting electric radiators.  

When direct‐acting electric radiators do make sense  
  – As a secondary or backup heat source in well-insulated buildings.  
  – In small spaces or rooms that are only occasionally used.  
  – Where installation of a central boiler or heat‐pump system isn’t practical.  

Tips to improve their performance if you choose to use them  
  – Install individual thermostats or electronic room‐by‐room controllers.  
  – Use programming or “smart” timers to ensure they only run when rooms are occupied.  
  – Ensure good insulation and air-sealing so that the heat you pay for isn’t lost immediately through walls, windows or roofs.  

Bottom line: Direct‐acting electric radiators are simple and deliver heat instantly, but because of higher electricity costs and poorer primary‐energy efficiency, they are rarely the most cost-effective or climate-friendly choice as a sole heating system in a building.

Here are several practical strategies to get the best performance and lowest running‐cost from direct‐acting electric radiators:

1. Install Individual Thermostatic Controls  
   • Fit each radiator with a digital or programmable thermostat valve (TRV) so you can set—and automatically maintain—the exact temperature in each room.  
   • Use setback schedules (e.g. lower overnight or when the house is empty) to avoid heating when you don’t need it.

2. Zone Your Heating  
   • Divide your dwelling into heating zones (living areas, bedrooms, bathrooms) on separate circuits or with separate timers.  
   • Only switch on and heat the zones you’re actually using rather than the whole building.

3. Fine-Tune Your Temperature Settings  
   • Reducing your room temperature by just 1 °C can save roughly 5–7 % on your heating bill.  
   • Aim for 18–20 °C in living areas and 16–18 °C in bedrooms.

4. Use Timers and Smart Controls  
   • Program your radiators to warm up shortly before you wake or return home—and to switch off or drop the temperature when you leave or go to bed.  
   • Consider smart or Wi-Fi–enabled controllers that let you adjust settings remotely via an app.

5. Leverage Off-Peak Tariffs (If Available)  
   • Some electricity suppliers offer night-time or weekend “off-peak” rates.  
   • Time your bulk heating (e.g. bringing water in the radiator up to temperature) to coincide with the cheaper periods.

6. Prevent Heat Loss  
   • Fit reflective foil panels behind each radiator to bounce heat back into the room rather than into an external wall.  
   • Seal drafts around windows and doors, and keep internal doors closed to contain warmth where you need it.

7. Maintain Clear Airflow  
   • Don’t cover or block the radiator with furniture, curtains or laundry racks.  
   • Give at least 10 cm clearance above and around the unit so warm air can circulate freely.

8. Ventilate Efficiently  
   • When airing rooms, open windows for short “burst” ventilation rather than leaving them half-open for long periods.  
   • Many radiators now offer “open-window detection” to pause heating automatically when a sudden heat drop is sensed.

9. Keep the Radiators Clean  
   • Dust and debris on fins or grill surfaces will reduce heat output.  
   • A quick wipe or vacuum brush a couple of times per year helps maintain efficiency.

10. Consider Complementary Insulation Measures  
    • Improving loft, wall or under-floor insulation reduces the work your electric radiators must do to maintain temperature.  
    • Even simple curtain liners and draught excluders around doors can make a noticeable difference to comfort and running cost.

By combining good controls (timers, thermostats, zoning) with sensible habits (lower set-points, quick airing) and basic building-fabric improvements, you can optimize the comfort and efficiency of direct-acting electric radiators—and keep your electricity bills as low as possible.

Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot-water systems typically involves reducing heat losses, ensuring high-efficiency heat generation, and matching output closely to demand. Here are the most common measures:

1. Improve Thermal Insulation  
   • Insulate the hot-water storage tank (min. 50–80 mm of closed-cell foam).  
   • Insulate all hot-water distribution pipes, including underfloor or ceiling runs, to reduce standby losses.  
   • Fit low-loss insulation on bends, valves and the tank’s top and bottom connections.

2. Use a High-Efficiency Heat Source  
   • Heat-pump water heaters: Coefficient of performance (COP) of 3–5, drawing low‐grade heat from air or ground.  
   • Condensing gas boilers: Achieve > 90 % seasonal efficiency by condensing flue gases.  
   • Electric on-demand (tankless) heaters: No tank losses, but electricity cost and peak-load demand should be considered.  

3. Pre-Heat with Renewables  
   • Solar thermal collectors: Pre-heat domestic hot water (DHW) by 30–70 % in sunny months.  
   • Heat recovery from greywater: Recover 40–60 % of the heat in discharged shower or bath water.

4. Optimize Control and Operation  
   • Lower the DHW set-point to 55 °C (or the minimum safe temperature) to reduce distribution losses.  
   • Install a timer or smart controller to switch off the heater during long periods of non-use.  
   • Use demand-controlled recirculation pumps—only operate when there is a call for hot water—to avoid constant loop losses.

5. Reduce Hot-Water Consumption  
   • Fit low-flow showerheads and faucet aerators to cut water and energy use by 30–50 %.  
   • Repair leaks promptly; a single drip can waste up to 15 litres per day.

6. Maintain Your System  
   • Flush tanks annually to remove sediment and scale, which reduce heat-exchange efficiency.  
   • Check insulation integrity and pipe lagging; replace or repair if damaged.  
   • Service burners or heat-pump units according to manufacturer recommendations.

By combining improved insulation, high-efficiency heat sources (or pre-heating with renewables), smart controls and reduced consumption, you can often cut domestic hot-water energy use by 30–60 % compared with an uninsulated, gas- or electric-resistance system operating continuously.

Optimizing domestic hot-water production in an apartment building involves both technical upgrades and operational best-practices. Below are several strategies you can consider:

1. High-efficiency generation  
   • Replace or supplement conventional boilers with energy-efficient heat pumps (air-to-water or ground-source).  
   • Consider condensing gas boilers sized correctly for the building’s simultaneous peak demand.  
   • If you have access to district heating, install a high-performance plate heat exchanger at the substation.  

2. Renewable integration  
   • Install solar-thermal collectors on the roof to preheat domestic hot water (DHW).  
   • Combine solar-thermal with an appropriately sized storage tank and control system for optimal utilization.  

3. Storage and stratification  
   • Use well-insulated hot-water storage tanks with internal stratification baffles to maintain differential temperatures.  
   • Minimize standby losses by choosing tanks with high-performance jackets (e.g., PIR or vacuum insulation).  

4. Distribution and controls  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipework and circulation loops to reduce heat losses.  
   • Fit variable-speed circulation pumps that adjust flow to actual demand rather than running continuously at full speed.  
   • Install time- and temperature-based control systems to turn circulation pumps on only when needed (e.g., mornings and evenings).  

5. Heat recovery  
   • Recover heat from draining showers and sinks by installing a heat-recovery unit in the wastewater drain line.  
   • In larger developments, consider heat recovery from ventilation exhaust air (if dual-duct MVHR is in place).  

6. Temperature management and safety  
   • Set storage-tank temperatures to the minimum safe level (usually around 55–60 °C) to limit heat losses, then use thermostatic mixing valves at draw-off points to deliver 40–45 °C to users.  
   • Carry out regular maintenance and descaling to ensure heat-exchanger efficiency and reduce corrosion.  

7. Monitoring and tenant engagement  
   • Fit individual meters or submeters for each apartment so residents can see their consumption and be incentivized to save.  
   • Provide simple guides to tenants on low-flow fixtures, shower timers or eco-modes to reduce unnecessary DHW use.  
   • Implement centralized monitoring (BMS or smart metering) to detect leaks, monitor performance and plan targeted maintenance.  

By combining efficient heat generation, minimized distribution losses, heat-recovery technologies and active monitoring/tenant engagement, you can significantly reduce energy use for domestic hot water while maintaining comfort and safety.

An energy declaration (in Swedish, “energideklaration”) is a legally required, standardized assessment of a building’s energy performance. It takes the form of an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and must be drawn up by an accredited energy expert whenever a building is constructed, sold or leased in Sweden. Key features include:  
• Energy classification: A graded scale (usually A–G) showing how energy-efficient the building is.  
• Measured energy use: Annual energy consumption expressed in kWh/m², based on heating, cooling, ventilation and hot water systems.  
• Building characteristics: Such data as heated floor area (Atemp), number of floors, building type and stairwells are recorded (e.g. using EPC fields like epc_egenatemp, epc_egenantalplan, etc.).  
• Technical installations: Information on heating, ventilation and cooling systems, insulation levels, window types, lighting, etc.  
• Improvement recommendations: A prioritized list of cost-effective measures (e.g. better insulation, upgrading windows, heat-pump installation) to reduce energy use and emissions.  
• Validity and compliance: The declaration is generally valid for ten years and must be submitted to the Swedish National Board of Housing, Building and Planning (Boverket).  

In summary, the energy declaration provides owners, buyers and tenants with transparent information on a building’s current energy performance and practical steps to improve its efficiency.

Energy-efficiency improvement in the context of buildings refers to any measure or combination of measures that reduces the amount of energy a building consumes while maintaining or improving its level of comfort, indoor air quality and functionality. In practice this typically means:

• Building envelope upgrades  
  – Adding or upgrading insulation in walls, roofs or floors  
  – Replacing or retrofitting windows and doors with higher-performance (e.g. low-E, triple-glazed) products  
  – Sealing air leaks and improving airtightness  

• HVAC and domestic hot water system enhancements  
  – Installing high-efficiency boilers, heat pumps or combined heat-and-power units  
  – Upgrading distribution systems (pumps, pipes, ducts) for lower losses  
  – Implementing heat-recovery ventilation  

• Lighting and controls  
  – Replacing incandescent or fluorescent lamps with LEDs  
  – Adding daylight sensors, occupancy controls and smart lighting systems  

• Building services automation  
  – Installing or improving building management systems (BMS) for optimized heating, cooling and ventilation scheduling  
  – Using smart thermostats, metering and sub-metering to monitor and control energy use  

• Renewable energy integration  
  – Adding photovoltaic panels or small wind turbines  
  – Incorporating solar thermal collectors for domestic hot water or space heating  

Each of these measures lowers the building’s overall energy demand, often reflected in an improved Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) rating or “energi­klass.” By systematically identifying, prioritizing and implementing such improvements—often starting with simple, low-cost measures and moving to deeper retrofits—a building owner can substantially reduce operating costs, carbon emissions and discomfort due to drafts or temperature fluctuations.

Properties can contain a variety of premises, each with its own typical energy‐use profile. Broadly speaking, you can divide them into these main categories:

1. Residential units  
   • Apartments, condominiums or single-family homes.  
   • Energy drivers: space heating, domestic hot water, appliances and lighting.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Moderate internal heat gains from occupants and appliances.  
     – Heating dominates in cold months; cooling (if any) is usually limited.  
     – Hot-water demand varies with number of residents and habits.

2. Office and administrative space  
   • Open-plan offices, individual offices, meeting rooms, reception areas.  
   • Energy drivers: lighting, computers and electronics, ventilation and comfort cooling.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Peak loads during normal working hours (often 8–18).  
     – High ventilation rates for indoor air quality.  
     – Moderate heating demand outside occupancy hours if unoccupied setbacks are used.

3. Retail and service premises  
   • Shops, showrooms, banks, hair salons, etc.  
   • Energy drivers: lighting (often high levels to display merchandise), heating or cooling, point-of-sale equipment.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Extended opening hours (some even 24/7).  
     – Significant lighting loads and sometimes refrigeration (in food stores).  
     – Variable heating or cooling depending on customer flow and display requirements.

4. Hospitality and restaurant space  
   • Restaurants, cafés, hotels, conference areas.  
   • Energy drivers: commercial cooking equipment, laundry (in hotels), ventilation and hot water.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Large hot-water demands in kitchens and laundries.  
     – Intensive ventilation to remove cooking odors and maintain comfort.  
     – Lighting and comfort heating/cooling for guest areas.

5. Healthcare and educational facilities  
   • Hospitals, clinics, schools, day-care centres.  
   • Energy drivers: intensive ventilation, sterilization or laboratory equipment, specialized lighting.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Continuous operation in hospitals with high HVAC loads.  
     – Schools have peak loads during school hours but generally lower overnight.

6. Industrial and warehouse space  
   • Factories, workshops, storage halls, logistic centres.  
   • Energy drivers: process machinery, large-volume heating or cooling, heavy-duty lighting.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Energy use dominated by production equipment or racking illumination.  
     – Heating may be zoned or on only when the space is in active use.  
     – Warehouses often have high ceilings and large air volumes, increasing heating/cooling loads.

7. Parking garages and technical rooms  
   • Underground or multi-storey parking; boiler rooms; plant rooms.  
   • Energy drivers: ventilation for exhaust removal, lighting, pump operation.  
   • Consumption characteristics:  
     – Continuous low-level lighting and ventilation.  
     – Technical rooms consume energy primarily for building services rather than comfort.

How premises type affects total energy consumption  
• Operating Hours: Longer opening times or 24/7 operation push up both base and peak energy loads.  
• Internal Gains: Premises with heavy equipment (kitchens, data centres, factories) generate more heat, sometimes reducing heating needs but increasing cooling demand.  
• Ventilation Requirements: Spaces with high occupancy density or pollutant loads need more air changes, driving up heating or cooling energy.  
• Temperature Set-Points: Comfort standards differ (offices ~21 °C, storage ~10 °C), directly influencing heating and cooling.  
• Hot-Water Demand: Residential and hospitality units often dominate the building’s hot-water energy share.  

When assessing or modelling a building’s energy performance— for example in an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)—you must identify each premise type, its floor area (Atemp) and its usage pattern. That allows you to allocate heating, cooling, ventilation and domestic-hot-water loads accurately and to target the most effective efficiency measures for each part of the property.

In multi-dwelling or commercial buildings, the bulk of electricity consumed in common areas typically covers the following functions:

1. Lighting  
   • Corridors and stairwells: often on 24/7 or activated by motion/timers for safety and way-finding.  
   • Lobbies and entrance halls: higher‐lux fixtures (pendants, downlights) may be on occupancy sensors or time clocks.  
   • Emergency and exit signage: maintained in “always-on” or battery-backed circuits.

2. Vertical transport (lifts and escalators)  
   • Traction motors and control electronics: draw power both in active travel and in standby (door-opening, control panels).  
   • Lighting and ventilation within lift cars and machine rooms.

3. Ventilation and smoke‐extraction fans  
   • Common‐area airhandling: intermittent or continuous duty fans in corridors and lobbies, especially in larger buildings.  
   • Fire-safety systems: high‐capacity smoke extraction fans (often tested regularly).

4. Pumps and hydraulic systems  
   • Fire-fighting pumps (wet risers, sprinkler systems): electrically driven, kept on standby.  
   • Domestic-hot-water circulation or heating‐system pumps serving common risers.

5. Security, access and communication  
   • Card-readers, intercoms, CCTV cameras and recording equipment.  
   • Door-operators (automatic sliding doors, electric access gates).

6. Building‐Management and Control Systems (BMS/BAS)  
   • Central controllers, sensors and gateways that monitor HVAC, lighting schedules and alarms.  
   • Network equipment (switches, routers) for remote monitoring.

Typical breakdown (varies by building size and use) might be: lighting 40–50 %, lifts 20–30 %, ventilation and pumps 15–20 %, plus 5–10 % for security and building‐management electronics. In modern energy-certified buildings (EPC class A–C), you will often find LED lighting with presence detectors, variable-speed drives on fans and lifts, and centralized BMS scheduling to minimize common-area kWh consumption.

Apartment buildings typically combine a range of envelope, system-level and user-oriented measures to boost their energy performance. Commonly implemented strategies include:

1. Building Envelope Improvements  
   • Insulation upgrades – adding or increasing thermal insulation in external walls, roofs and basement ceilings.  
   • High-performance windows and doors – replacing single- or double-glazed units with low-U-value, triple-glazed frames and thermally broken profiles.  
   • Air-tightness enhancements – sealing joints, penetrations and service ducts to reduce uncontrolled drafts and heat losses.

2. Heating, Ventilation and Cooling (HVAC) Upgrades  
   • Condensing boilers or high-efficiency heat pumps – modern gas, oil or electric heat pumps with seasonal efficiency (SCOP) ratings above 3.0.  
   • District heating optimization – installation of individual sub-stations or smart control valves to better match heat delivery to demand.  
   • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) – balanced system that recovers up to 80 % of the exhaust air’s heat, supplying fresh, pre-warmed air.  
   • Variable-speed drives and smart controls – electronically commutated motors (ECMs) and demand-controlled ventilation based on CO₂ or humidity sensors.

3. Renewable and Low-Carbon Generation  
   • Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels – roof- or façade-mounted arrays sized to match common areas or tenant loads.  
   • Solar thermal collectors – pre-heating domestic hot water or supplementing the central heating circuit.  
   • Heat pump integration – hybrid solutions combining ground-source or air-source heat pumps with existing boilers.

4. Lighting and Electrical Systems  
   • LED fixtures – replacing fluorescent or incandescent lamps throughout stairwells, corridors and common rooms.  
   • Occupancy and daylight sensors – automatically dimming or switching off lights in unoccupied spaces.  
   • Energy-efficient motors and pumps – for circulation and lift systems, often with frequency inverters.

5. Hot Water and Distribution  
   • Insulated hot-water storage and distribution pipes – minimizing standby losses.  
   • Smart metering and sub-metering – allowing tenants to monitor and adjust their own consumption patterns.  
   • On-demand (instantaneous) water heaters – reducing storage losses in smaller buildings.

6. Building Automation and Energy Management  
   • Central Building Management Systems (BMS) – integrating HVAC, lighting, shading and metering for performance optimization.  
   • Smart thermostats and zone controls – providing residents with precise temperature settings and scheduling.  
   • Fault detection and diagnostics – remote monitoring to identify performance deviations or equipment failures early.

7. Resident Engagement and Behavioral Measures  
   • Information campaigns and dashboards – educating occupants on simple actions (window-opening habits, thermostat settings).  
   • Incentive programs – rewarding energy-saving practices or on-time payment to support maintenance of efficient systems.

By combining envelope, system-level and user-centric actions, apartment buildings can typically improve their EPC energy class by one or more steps (for example from class D to class B), reduce operating costs and cut carbon emissions by 20–50 %, depending on the scope of measures and the building’s starting condition.

In most residential and commercial buildings, the largest electricity‐consuming end-uses typically are:

1. Space heating (when electric)  
   – Includes direct electric radiators, underfloor heating or heat-pump compressors.  
   – Can account for 30–60 % of a building’s total electricity load in cold climates if no district or central heating is used.

2. Domestic hot water  
   – Electric boilers or heat-pump water heaters supply showers, washing machines and faucets.  
   – Often 10–25 % of total consumption.

3. Ventilation, pumps and fans  
   – Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery, circulation pumps for hydronic systems and booster fans in larger buildings.  
   – Typically 5–15 %.

4. Space cooling  
   – Air-conditioning compressors or reversible heat-pumps in warmer climates.  
   – Shares vary widely (5–20 % or more during hot seasons).

5. Lighting  
   – Interior and exterior lighting fixtures.  
   – Around 5–15 % of annual electricity use, declining with widespread LED adoption.

6. Appliances and plug loads  
   – Refrigerators, freezers, laundry machines, dishwashers, TVs, computers and other electronics.  
   – Generally 10–20 % of a household’s electricity.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house is largely a matter of encouraging air to flow where and when you need it, without resorting to mechanical fans or heat recovery units. The following strategies can help you achieve effective, energy-free ventilation:

1. Orient and size your openings for cross-ventilation  
   • Place operable windows or vents on opposite or adjacent walls to create a clear airflow path.  
   • Make sure each principal room (living room, bedrooms) has at least two opening points.  
   • Use larger openings on the windward side and slightly smaller ones on the leeward side to maintain positive pressure inlets and negative pressure outlets.

2. Exploit the stack (buoyancy) effect  
   • Incorporate high‐level vents, skylights or roof hatches that can be opened to let warm air rise and escape.  
   • In multi-storey buildings, stack effect can be enhanced by creating vertical shafts or “solar chimneys” that capture solar heat to drive upward airflow.  
   • Ensure any vertical ducting or stairwell used for ventilation is well sealed from unintended air leaks but open when you want to purge heat.

3. Use adjustable trickle vents and door grilles  
   • Trickle vents (small controllable in-window vents) allow background ventilation even when windows are closed, improving air quality without drafts.  
   • Door-under-cut grilles or transfer grilles help distribute air between rooms and prevent pressure imbalances that could draw air through unintended gaps.

4. Integrate passive solar and night‐time cooling  
   • In warm seasons, open low‐level openings in the evening or early morning (when outdoor air is coolest) and high-level vents at night to flush heat out of the structure.  
   • Close or shade openings during the daytime peak to avoid excess solar gains.

5. Provide unobstructed flow paths  
   • Keep furniture or curtains away from vents and windows.  
   • Design interior partitions and circulation zones (corridors, stairwells) to act as low-resistance air highways when doors are open.

6. Match ventilation strategy to building envelope tightness  
   • A relatively airtight envelope helps you control airflow through deliberate openings, rather than through random cracks.  
   • Seal unintended gaps (around windows, doors, service penetrations) so that all fresh air comes in where you’ve designed for it.

7. Consider landscaping and site factors  
   • Use shrubs or fences as wind deflectors to slow and smooth prevailing breezes before they reach your inlets.  
   • Avoid placing vents directly opposite large obstacles (garage doors, outbuildings) that could create eddies.

8. Balance thermal comfort and air quality  
   • In cold climates, limit full window openings to milder periods to avoid discomfort.  
   • Incorporate humidity control (e.g., operable louvers in wet rooms) so that moisture doesn’t accumulate.

By combining cross-ventilation, the stack effect and controlled trickle‐vent systems, you can maintain good indoor air quality, avoid overheating in summer, and minimize heating needs in winter—all without relying on powered fans or ducted systems.

When you’re evaluating whether to invest in a rooftop or ground-mounted solar photovoltaic (PV) system, you should consider the following key factors:

1. Solar resource and roof characteristics  
   • Orientation and tilt – South-facing roofs with a tilt of 25–40° produce the most energy in Sweden.

   • Roof condition and age – An older roof may need replacing before panels go up.  
   • Load-bearing capacity – Verify that rafters/trusses can carry the extra weight of panels, rails and snow loads.  

3. Your energy consumption and system sizing  
   • Annual electricity use – Review past bills to size the PV array so that generation matches or slightly exceeds your needs.  
   • Future changes – If you plan to buy an electric vehicle or add electric heating, factor in higher consumption.  

4. Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and efficiency  
   • EPC energy class (epc_egienergiklass) – A high (efficient) class means your building uses less power for heating and cooling, so you’ll need a smaller PV system to cover consumption.  

5. Financial considerations and incentives  
   • Up-front cost – Equipment, installation and grid-connection fees.  
   • Subsidies and tax rebates – Sweden offers investment support (investeringsstöd) and a tax reduction for small producers (60 öre/kWh).  
   • Net metering or feed-in tariffs – Check your local grid operator’s rules for exporting excess electricity.  
   • Return on investment and payback period – Typically 8–12 years in Sweden, depending on incentives and electricity prices.  

6. Equipment quality and warranties  
   • Solar panels – Look for 25-year performance warranties and reputable manufacturers.  
   • Inverters – Central or micro-inverters; most come with 10- to 15-year warranties.

By carefully evaluating your roof’s suitability, your building’s energy performance (including its EPC energy class), your electricity needs and the financial incentives available, you’ll be able to size a PV system correctly, optimize your return on investment and ensure a reliable, long-lasting solar installation.

The building’s energy class (the “epc_egienergiklass” in an energy performance certificate) is a snapshot of how efficiently it uses energy overall—taking into account insulation, ventilation, heating and cooling systems, windows, etc. Although the EPC grade itself does not prescribe specific appliance models, it strongly influences how you should select household appliances if your goal is to optimize a building’s total energy consumption and running costs. Here’s how:

1. Balancing Building performance and Appliance efficiency  
   • A- or B-rated building: you already have a well-insulated envelope and efficient HVAC systems. You can further reduce energy use by choosing top-tier appliances (formerly A+++ under the EU label, now A or B under the 2021-2028 scale) such as inverter-driven refrigerators, front-loading heat-pump dryers and induction cooktops.  
   • D- to G-rated building: your building loses more energy through walls, windows or heating distribution. To compensate, it becomes even more important to select appliances with the highest available efficiency—especially those with eco-modes, smart-grid compatibility or demand-response features—to limit additional energy strain.

2. Size and Capacity  
   • Match appliance capacity to household needs: oversizing a refrigerator, dishwasher or washing machine can lead to unnecessary cycle energy waste.  
   • In a large, well-insulated home you might afford a larger but still energy-efficient model; in a poorly rated (lower-class) building you may prefer smaller units or those with variable-load technology.

3. Synergy with Building Services  
   • Smart meters and energy-management systems often accompany higher-rated buildings. Choose appliances that can integrate with these systems (Wi-Fi, Zigbee, etc.) to schedule cycles during off-peak or when on-site PV generation is high.  
   • In a lower-rated building, prioritise appliances that reach their high-efficiency performance at lower temperatures or shorter cycles (e.g., eco-washing programs).

4. Long-Term Cost vs. Purchase Price  
   • In a building with a strong EPC class, the incremental savings from a premium-rated appliance may be smaller but still worthwhile for net zero goals.  
   • In a poor-class building, energy costs are higher overall—so investing in the very best energy-labelled appliances often pays back faster in reduced utility bills.

5. Regulatory and Funding Incentives  
   • Some renovation or energy-retrofit incentives require you to maintain or improve your EPC class. When you upgrade appliances, selecting top-rated models will help you document those improvements and qualify for subsidies or favourable financing.

In practice, always consult the latest EU energy-label scale (A to G) when shopping for refrigerators, dishwashers, washing machines, etc. Align your appliance choices with the building’s EPC rating: the lower the class, the more you benefit from choosing the highest-efficiency models available.

To estimate the total electrical power demand in your home, follow these steps:

1. Inventory All Electrical Loads  
   • List every appliance and system that draws electricity – e.g. lighting circuits, refrigeration, cooking appliances, HVAC (heating/ventilation/air-conditioning), water heaters, laundry machines, entertainment equipment, electric vehicle chargers, etc.  
   • Don’t forget occasional or seasonal loads (e.g. heat pumps, dehumidifiers, holiday lighting).

2. Record Name-Plate Ratings  
   • For each item, note its maximum power rating (in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW)) as shown on the device’s nameplate or in the user manual.  
   • If only current (amps) is given, calculate power: P (kW) = U (volts) × I (amps) ÷ 1 000.

3. Apply Diversity/Simultaneity Factors  
   • In reality, not all appliances run at full power or at the same time. Many electrical‐load calculations apply a “diversity factor” or “simultaneity factor” to reflect typical usage.  
   • For a rough estimate, you can use 100 % for major continuous loads (e.g. fridge, freezer, electric heating) and perhaps 50–75 % for intermittent loads (e.g. microwave, vacuum cleaner). National or local electrical codes often provide recommended diversity tables.

4. Sum Up the Loads  
   • Add together all the adjusted (diversified) power ratings to get your design or peak power demand, in kW.  
   • Example:  
     • HVAC: 6 kW × 1.0 = 6 kW  
     • Lighting and outlets: 4 kW × 0.75 = 3 kW  
     • Kitchen appliances: 5 kW × 0.6 = 3 kW  
     • Miscellaneous: 2 kW × 0.5 = 1 kW  
     Total ≈ 13 kW peak demand

5. Verify with Measurement (Optional)  
   • Install a whole-house energy monitor or clamp-on meter at your main service panel.  
   • Record the instantaneous demand over a representative period (e.g. a few days) to capture peak loads and verify your calculated values.

6. Distinguish Power Demand vs. Energy Consumption  
   • Power demand (kW) is the instantaneous load you size your service and wiring for.  
   • Energy consumption (kWh) is the integral of power over time and determines your utility bill. To estimate energy, multiply each device’s power by the expected operating hours.

Tips for Accuracy  
- Consult a qualified electrician or energy consultant if you need a precise load calculation for HVAC sizing or electrical permit applications.  
- Use manufacturer’s data and local code guidance on diversity factors.  
- Account for future additions (e.g. EV charger, solar inverter) by leaving some headroom in your calculation.

Electricity bills in Sweden (and in most other markets) are made up of several components, and your actual usage directly determines the variable (energy-based) part of what you pay. Here’s how it all fits together:

1. Energy-component (kronor per kWh)  
   • You pay for every kilowatt-hour (kWh) you consume. If you use more electricity, this line-item on your bill grows in direct proportion.  
   • Many suppliers link their energy price to the Nord Pool spot price, plus a small margin and any costs for green certificates.  
   • Some contracts have block or tiered pricing—e.g. the first 2,000 kWh in a year at one rate, and any consumption above that at a higher rate.  

2. Time-of-use tariffs  
   • If you’ve chosen a time-of-use (ToU) or “natt-och-helg” (night & weekend) contract, your kWh rate varies by hour or by block (peak vs. off-peak).  
   • Shifting high-consumption activities (laundry, EV-charging, heat pumps) to off-peak hours can materially reduce your average price per kWh.  

3. Grid fee (nätavgift)  
   • This covers the cost of maintaining and operating the local distribution grid. It normally has two parts:  
     – A fixed monthly fee (regardless of how much you use)  
     – A variable capacity or volume-based fee (either per kWh or per ampere of peak load)  
   • Your total consumption can influence the variable part, and very high peak loads can sometimes trigger higher capacity charges.  

4. Taxes and VAT  
   • Electricity tax (“energiskatt”) is levied per kWh consumed.  
   • Value-added tax (25 % in Sweden) is charged on the sum of the energy component, grid fees and energy tax.  

Summary:  
– Every extra kWh you draw adds directly to the energy component of your bill (and increases your energy tax).  
– If you’re on a block-tariff or ToU contract, the price per kWh may rise once you pass certain thresholds or during peak hours.  
– Reducing your overall consumption—or shifting it to off-peak periods—lowers both your energy charges and the percentage-based taxes and fees.

In most liberalized electricity markets (for example, in Sweden and many other countries), you in fact need two separate agreements in order to have power in your home or business. They cover different parts of “getting electricity” to you:

1. Grid contract (Network agreement)  
   • Who you sign with: Your local grid or distribution system operator (DSO). This is the company that owns and maintains the wires, poles, transformers and metering equipment in your area.  
   • What it covers:  
     – The right to use the distribution network to transmit electricity between the national transmission grid and your property.  
     – Grid fees, which pay for construction, maintenance and operation of the local grid. These fees are typically regulated by a national authority (e.g. Energimarknadsinspektionen in Sweden) and consist of a fixed charge plus a volumetric charge per kWh.  
     – Metering and grid services (connection point, meter reading, customer support in case of outages).  
   • Why it’s necessary: Even if you generate your own power (solar panels, small wind), you still need a grid connection to import/export electricity or to be backed up by the broader system.  

2. Electricity supply contract (Retail or energy agreement)  
   • Who you sign with: A licensed electricity supplier or trader. You can typically choose among many competing suppliers on the open market.  
   • What it covers:  
     – The procurement and sale of the actual energy (electricity) you consume. Suppliers purchase electricity on wholesale markets or through bilateral contracts and resell it to end customers.  
     – The price components: energy price (often variable or fixed), taxes and levies (e.g. electricity tax, VAT), and any supplier fees.  
     – Optional product features: green‐energy guarantees of origin, fixed‐price or spot‐price contracts, dynamic pricing, etc.  
   • Why it’s necessary: Without an electricity supply contract you would not be billed for the kilowatt‐hours you consume, and suppliers would have no commercial incentive to procure your power.  

How the two work together  
 - You must have a grid contract to physically receive electricity and to be metered.  
 - You must also have an electricity supply contract to legally purchase the energy and to receive an electricity bill that covers your consumption.  
 - Even if you switch supplier, your grid agreement remains with the same local DSO (unless you move), so your power delivery is unaffected.  
 - When you move into a new property, you must both establish a grid contract (if one isn’t already active) and choose an electricity supplier.  

In short:  
– The grid contract gives you physical access to the wires and infrastructure.  
– The electricity supply contract provides you with the commodity (the kilowatt‐hours) and determines what you pay per unit of energy.

Control and regulation technology (sometimes called “styr- och reglarteknik” in Swedish) is the collection of methods, devices and systems used to monitor, control and optimise technical processes. In the context of buildings and energy performance, it typically includes:

1. Sensors and Transmitters  
   • Measure physical or environmental parameters such as temperature, humidity, CO₂ concentration, pressure and flow.  
   • Provide real-time data for the control system.

2. Controllers and Control Loops  
   • Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), direct digital controllers (DDCs) or dedicated HVAC controllers execute control algorithms (e.g. on/off, proportional–integral–derivative or “PID” control).  
   • Continuously compare measured values against set-points and calculate corrective actions.

3. Actuators and Final Control Elements  
   • Valves, dampers, variable-speed drives (VSDs) on pumps and fans, electric heaters or chillers that carry out the adjustments dictated by the controller.  
   • Open or close, speed up or slow down to bring the process variable back to its set-point.

4. Building Management System (BMS) or Building Automation System (BAS)  
   • A supervisory layer that collects data from multiple controllers and sensors.  
   • Provides scheduling, trend logging, alarm management and user interfaces (graphical dashboards, touch panels or web portals).  
   • Enables remote monitoring and optimisation of energy use, comfort and indoor air quality.

5. Communication and Integration  
   • Standardised protocols (BACnet, Modbus, KNX, LON, etc.) allow devices from different manufacturers to exchange data.  
   • Integration with other building systems—lighting, security, fire protection and renewable energy installations—for coordinated operation.

Why it matters for buildings  
• Energy Efficiency: By continuously adjusting heating, cooling and ventilation to actual demand, you minimise wasted energy.  
• Comfort and Indoor Climate: Stable temperatures, correct humidity and fresh air levels improve occupant wellbeing and productivity.  
• Operational Reliability: Automated monitoring and alarming reduce the risk of equipment failure and allow for proactive maintenance.  
• Sustainability and Certification: Properly commissioned and maintained control systems are often prerequisites for energy-label certifications (e.g. EPC) and green building standards (LEED, BREEAM, Miljöbyggnad).

In short, control and regulation technology is the “brains and nerves” behind modern building services—it senses conditions, makes decisions and drives equipment so that buildings operate safely, comfortably and as energy-efficiently as possible.

Expanding a control system typically involves both hardware and software considerations, as well as careful planning to ensure reliability, performance and maintainability as you add new functionality. Below is a step-by-step outline of a typical expansion process:

1. Clarify Expansion Objectives  
   – Identify exactly what new processes, machines or functions must be controlled.  
   – Define performance requirements (e.g. faster response time, higher I/O counts, improved data logging).  

2. Review Existing Architecture  
   – Map out your current controller hierarchy (PLCs, PACs, DCS, SCADA, edge devices).  
   – Inventory available spare I/O slots, communication ports and CPU capacity.  
   – Evaluate network topology and bandwidth headroom.

3. Hardware Expansion  
   – I/O Modules: add remote or local I/O racks/modules to accommodate new sensors and actuators.  
   – Controllers: if the existing CPU is at capacity, add parallel or higher-performance controllers.  
   – Network Infrastructure: extend Ethernet switches, fiber or industrial fieldbus segments (e.g. PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, Modbus TCP).  

4. Software and Configuration  
   – Modular Design: encapsulate new control logic in separate function blocks or objects for maintainability.  
   – Communication Setup: configure new device addresses, update routing tables, and ensure protocol compatibility (OPC UA, MQTT, etc.).  
   – HMI/SCADA: extend operator screens, alarms and trends to include new signals and control loops.  

5. Scalability and Hierarchy  
   – Consider a multi-tiered approach: local controllers handle high-speed interlocks, while supervisory systems oversee recipe management and analytics.  
   – For very large or geographically dispersed systems, introduce edge controllers or IIoT gateways to offload data processing.

6. Integration and Interoperability  
   – Verify vendor compatibility for added modules or controllers.  
   – Use open standards where possible to avoid future lock-in and to simplify firmware/software upgrades.

7. Testing and Commissioning  
   – Factory Acceptance Test (FAT): simulate new I/O and control logic in a test bench before on-site work.  
   – Site Acceptance Test (SAT): perform stepwise commissioning—first dry runs, then live process tests under supervision.  
   – Safety Validation: re-evaluate safety interlocks, emergency stops and functional safety compliance (e.g. SIL levels).

8. Documentation and Training  
   – Update system architecture diagrams, I/O lists, network maps and software manuals.  
   – Train operators and maintenance staff on the new components, HMI changes and troubleshooting procedures.

9. Ongoing Maintenance and Monitoring

In the electric-vehicle industry today, charging modes are generally categorised by the power delivered (measured in kilowatts, kW) and by whether the current is alternating (AC) or direct (DC). Although definitions can vary slightly from country to country and between manufacturers, the following breakdown is widely used:

1. Slow or “Trickle” Charging (AC)  
  • Power: up to 3.7 kW (single-phase)  
  • Typical use: home wall-boxes or domestic sockets  
  • Charging speed: adds roughly 10–15 km of range per charging hour  

2. Normal (or “Fast”) AC Charging  
  • Power: 3.7 – 22 kW (single-phase up to 7.4 kW; three-phase up to 22 kW)  
  • Typical use: workplace charging, public AC chargers  
  • Charging speed: adds roughly 20–60 km of range per charging hour  

3. High-Power (DC) Fast Charging  
  • Power: 50 kW and above (DC)  
  • Typical use: motorway service areas, dedicated rapid-charge stations  
  • Charging speed: adds roughly 200–300 km of range in 20–30 minutes  

4. Ultra-Fast Charging  
  • Power: 150 kW to 350 kW (or higher) (DC)  
  • Typical use: cutting-edge public chargers for long-distance travel  
  • Charging speed: adds 200–300 km in 10–15 minutes, depending on vehicle capability  

Boundary Between “Normal” and “Fast” Charging  
– In the AC domain, “normal” charging usually tops out at around 22 kW; anything above that (when you switch to DC) is considered fast charging.  
– By international convention, DC charging stations rated at 50 kW or more are termed “fast chargers.” Ultra-fast chargers start around 150 kW.  

Therefore, the practical boundary between normal (AC) charging and fast (DC) charging is:  
  • AC ≤ 22 kW = Normal (or Fast-AC) charging  
  • DC ≥ 50 kW = Fast charging (with ultra-fast at ≥150 kW)

Load balancing for electric-vehicle (EV) charging is the process of managing and distributing available electrical power among one or more charging points so that you:

• Stay within the capacity limits of your building’s electrical installation (service main, distribution boards, cable ratings)  
• Avoid tripping breakers or exceeding feeder capacities  
• Optimize energy use, for example by shifting load to times of lower overall demand or to on-site renewable generation  

Key aspects of EV-charging load balancing  
1. Static vs. Dynamic Balancing  
   – Static balancing allocates a fixed maximum current to each charger (e.g. 32 A), based on the panel’s rating. It’s simple but can be inefficient if some chargers are unused.  
   – Dynamic balancing continuously monitors overall site load (and in some systems, even total grid import) and adjusts each individual charger’s current in real time.  

2. Local (Phase) Balancing  
   – In three-phase electrical systems, you can shift EV loads between phases to keep each phase draw balanced. This avoids overloading one phase, which would otherwise cause voltage imbalance or breaker trips.  

3. Master-Slave or Networked Architectures  
   – Master-Slave (daisy-chain) systems: one “master” charger measures total current and tells the “slave” units how much they may draw.  
   – Networked (typically OCPP-based) systems: each charger communicates with a central controller (on-premises or cloud) that orchestrates charge currents based on real-time data from all chargers and from the building management system (BMS).  

4. Grid-Aware and Time-of-Use Optimization  
   – Advanced load-balancing systems can factor in dynamic electricity tariffs, grid-import limits, or signals from the Distribution System Operator (DSO) to reduce costs and maximize renewable self-consumption.  
   – You can program charging to ramp up when solar PV production is high or when off-peak utility rates apply, and to slow down or pause when demand elsewhere in the building is high.  

5. Benefits  
   – Safety and Compliance: prevents overloads and nuisance trips, ensuring you stay within approved cable and breaker ratings.  
   – Cost Efficiency: more vehicles can be served with the same electrical infrastructure, delaying or eliminating costly upgrades.  
   – Grid Support: by smoothing peaks and integrating with demand-response programs, load balancing helps stabilize the grid and can even generate revenue or lower energy bills.  
   – User Experience: drivers get more reliable, predictable charging sessions—chargers don’t simply shut off when the panel capacity is reached.  

In practice, choosing the right load-balancing solution depends on your site’s size, number of chargers, existing electrical capacity, and whether you need integration with your building’s energy-management system or with external smart-grid programs. Modern smart chargers and management platforms make it relatively straightforward to implement both simple phase balancing and full dynamic load management across many vehicles.

In Sweden there are several national‐ and regional-level programmes that can help cover part of the cost of upgrading the insulation in an apartment building. The main options today are:

1. ROT-deduction (ROT-avdrag)  
   • You as a property owner can deduct 30 % of the labour cost (labour and travel) for renovation or energy-saving measures, including new insulation in walls, roof or floor.   
   • You apply directly via your tax return (pre-notification to the Tax Agency). Materials must be paid in full; the deduction only applies to the service portion of the invoice.  

2. Climate Leap (“Klimatklivet”)  
   • Administered by the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency (Naturvårdsverket).  
   • Provides investment support of up to 70 % of eligible project costs for larger, climate-benefitting measures. Insulation upgrades in multi-unit dwellings can qualify if they significantly reduce CO₂ emissions.  
   • Calls for proposals are published a few times per year. Decisions are made on a first-come, first-served basis, so it’s important to submit your application as soon as a call opens.

3. Investment support for energy efficiency in multi-family houses (Energimyndighetens stöd till flerbostadshus)  
   • Managed by the Swedish Energy Agency (Energimyndigheten).  
   • Covers up to 30 % of eligible costs for energy-saving renovations, including added wall, roof or floor insulation, upgraded windows/doors and installation of heat recovery ventilation.  
   • Typically you submit an energy-audit-based renovation plan; the grant is paid out once works are completed and documented.

4. Green loans and municipal housing funds  
   • Many municipalities (via regional energy offices) offer low-interest “green loans” for energy retrofits in apartment buildings.  
   • Check with your local municipality or regional county administrative board (länsstyrelse) for small-scale grants or supplementary financing.  

5. EU-co-financed programmes  
   • In some regions, you may find co-financing through Structural Funds (e.g. ERDF), especially if your building is in a designated less-developed area.  
   • Application rules and availability vary widely — check your regional development authority’s website.  

Key action steps:  
- Have an energy audit (energideklaration or voluntary energy survey) carried out to document current performance and calculate savings.  
- Contact the Swedish Energy Agency and Naturvårdsverket before you begin planning to confirm which calls are open and to get help in drafting your application.  
- Retain detailed quotations and invoices for both material and labour, since both grant bodies and the Tax Agency will require complete cost breakdowns.  

Because application windows, rates and eligibility rules can change from year to year, always consult the administering authority’s latest guidelines before you commit to a renovation plan.

Improving basement lighting typically requires a combination of maximizing available natural light (where possible) and installing well-designed artificial lighting that meets both functional and aesthetic needs. Below are several strategies you can consider:

1. Introduce or enlarge daylight sources  
   – Window wells and light shafts (“light tubes” or “sun tunnels”) can capture daylight from ground level and pipe it into the basement ceiling.  
   – If structural work is an option, consider adding egress or hopper windows—these let in more daylight and improve ventilation and safety.  

2. Use high-efficiency, high-quality artificial fixtures  
   – LED fixtures: Choose LED lamps or panels with a high luminous efficacy (at least 100 lm/W) to keep energy use low.  
   – Color temperature & CRI: Select a color temperature in the 3000–4000 K range for a neutral-white light that feels natural, and a Color Rendering Index (CRI) of 80 or above to render colors accurately.  
   – Diffused lighting: Recessed or surface-mounted fixtures with frosted lenses reduce glare and distribute light evenly across the space.  

3. Implement a layered lighting scheme  
   – Ambient lighting: Ceiling-mounted fixtures or linear LED strips provide general illumination.  
   – Task lighting: Under-cabinet lights, floor lamps or adjustable wall-mounted fixtures focus light where you need it—e.g., workbenches, laundry areas, or desk spaces.  
   – Accent lighting: Wall sconces, picture lights or LED tape under shelving add depth and reduce the “dungeon” feel common in basements.  

4. Optimize reflectance and finishes  
   – Paint walls and ceilings in light-reflective colors (white or pastel tones) with a satin or eggshell finish to bounce light around the room.  
   – Use glossy or semi-gloss finishes sparingly on trim or moldings to add subtle reflections without creating hot spots.  
   – Incorporate mirrors or metallic accents strategically—these can multiply both natural and artificial light.  

5. Incorporate smart controls and zoning  
   – Occupancy sensors or motion detectors prevent lights from being left on in seldom-used areas.  
   – Dimmers and multi-scene switches let you adjust the lighting level for different activities (e.g., playroom, home gym, storage).  
   – Daylight harvesting controls (if you have daylight tubes or windows) modulate artificial lighting in response to natural light levels.  

6. Meet safety and code requirements  
   – Ensure emergency egress routes and stairways are illuminated at a minimum of 50 lux (per many building codes).  
   – Install emergency-rated exit signs or battery-backed lights in hallways and near staircases.  
   – Verify that all fixtures in potentially damp basement zones are rated for “damp” or “wet” locations as appropriate.  

By combining daylight-enhancing measures, efficient LED technology, layered fixture placement, reflective finishes and intelligent controls, you can transform a dark basement into a bright, welcoming and safe space.

Improving a building’s energy efficiency is best approached in stages, moving from the “fabric” of the building (walls, roof, windows, airtightness) to building services (heating, ventilation, lighting) and finally to renewable energy generation and energy management. Below are the key areas you should consider – you can adjust the priorities based on your current energy performance certificate (EPC) energy class (e.g. if you are in class E–G, strengthening the building envelope will generally deliver the biggest gains; if you are already in class A–C, focus on system optimization and renewables).

1. Building Envelope  
 • Insulation: Add or upgrade insulation in the roof/attic, external walls and—where accessible—the basement or ground floor slab. Even modest U-value improvements can cut heat losses by 20–30 %.  
 • Windows and doors: Replace single-glazed or poorly sealed units with high-performance double or triple glazing. Ensure good quality frames (low-conductivity materials) and airtight seals.  
 • Airtightness and draught reduction: Conduct an airtightness test (blower-door) and seal gaps around windows, doors, service penetrations and between building elements. Controlled ventilation (see below) will then provide fresh air without uncontrolled losses.

2. Heating, Cooling & Ventilation Systems  
 • Heating system upgrade: If you have an old oil or gas boiler, consider a modern condensing boiler or, ideally, a ground- or air-source heat pump. Heat pumps can typically operate with 200–400 % efficiency (relative to electrical input).  
 • Hot water system: Insulate hot water tanks and pipes, fit thermostatic mixing valves, and consider solar thermal pre-heating if you have suitable roof area.  
 • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR): Replaces extract fans with a balanced system that recovers up to 90 % of the heat from exhaust air while supplying filtered, tempered fresh air. Particularly important after improving airtightness.

3. Lighting, Controls & Appliances  
 • LED lighting: Replace all incandescent, halogen or fluorescent fixtures with LED lamps. LEDs consume 50–75 % less electricity and have much longer lifetimes.  
 • Smart controls and sensors: Install occupancy and daylight sensors, programmable thermostats and zoning controls so you only heat and light spaces when they are in use.  
 • Efficient appliances: Where possible, swap out old appliances (e.g. refrigerators, dishwashers, pumps) for A+++-rated models.

4. Renewable Energy & On-Site Generation  
 • Solar photovoltaics (PV): A rooftop or façade-mounted PV system can offset a large share of your building’s electricity consumption, improving your overall energy class.  
 • Solar thermal: As mentioned, solar collectors for hot water can reduce your heating load further.  
 • Battery storage: Pairing PV with storage lets you maximize self-consumption and reduce peak electricity costs.

5. Energy Monitoring & Management  
 • Sub-metering: Install meters on heating, hot water, ventilation and major circuits so you can identify the biggest users of energy and track improvements.  
 • Building management systems (BMS): In larger buildings, a BMS can optimize plant operation, schedule maintenance and prevent energy waste.  
 • Occupant engagement: Educate and incentivize users to adopt energy-wise behaviors (e.g. thermostat setbacks, turning off lights).

Next Steps  
1. Review your latest EPC (epc_egienergiklass): it will identify your current energy grade and specific weak spots.  
2. Commission a qualified energy auditor or building physicist to carry out a detailed survey, including thermography and airtightness testing.  
3. Develop a phased retrofit plan, starting with low-cost, high-impact measures (draught-proofing, LED lighting), then moving to envelope upgrades, system replacement and finally renewables.  

By following a holistic approach—improving the building fabric, optimizing systems and adding renewables—you’ll raise your energy class, reduce operating costs and lower your carbon footprint.

Here are several strategies to reduce standby (vampire) power in shared spaces such as meeting rooms, lounges, corridors and kitchens:  

1. Audit and identify  
   • Perform an inventory of all electrical devices that draw power when “off” or in sleep mode (e.g. TVs, AV‐equipment, vending machines, coffee makers, phone chargers).  
   • Use plug‐in energy meters for a spot check of high-consumption items.  

2. Centralize and automate switching  
   • Install master power switches or smart power strips—one click (or one schedule) turns off all devices in a zone.  
   • Deploy timers or building management system (BMS) schedules to cut power after hours or during prolonged idle periods.  

3. Use presence and daylight sensors  
   • In corridors and rest areas, fit motion detectors so lighting and small plug loads (e.g. networked printers) are only live when people are present.  
   • Combine with daylight harvesting to dim or switch off lights when enough natural light is available.  

4. Optimize equipment settings  
   • Enable energy-saving or deep-sleep modes on computers, screens and AV gear. Verify “wake-on-LAN” is disabled if not required.  
   • Where applicable, upgrade firmware so devices enter lower-power states more aggressively.  

5. Upgrade to energy-efficient hardware  
   • Replace legacy power supplies and chargers with units certified to have very low standby draw (look for “no load” or <0.1 W idle rating).  
   • Choose ENERGY STAR® or equivalent appliances and electronics.  

6. Staff engagement and policies  
   • Post clear signage in shared areas (“Please switch off equipment at the end of the day”).  
   • Circulate simple guidelines on how to shut down projectors, screens and kitchen appliances properly.  
   • Assign “energy champions” to periodically verify compliance.  

7. Ongoing monitoring and review  
   • Track overall common-area consumption on your submeter or building energy management platform.  
   • Benchmark performance and set quarterly targets for reducing standby losses.  

By combining behavioral measures, automated controls and more efficient equipment, you can typically cut standby consumption in shared spaces by 50 % or more—often paying back any small control‐hardware investment within a year.

Before embarking on a solar-panel installation, a building board should systematically verify the following points:

1. Legal and regulatory requirements  
   • Planning permission (bygglov) or notification to your municipality – check local building-code rules, especially if you’re in a conservation area.  
   • Homeowners’ association or condominium statutes – ensure the project has been approved by the required quorum of owners.  
   • National grid‐connection rules and permits – coordinate with your electricity network operator for net-metering/injection approval.

2. Roof and structural suitability  
   • Roof condition and remaining service life – panels typically last 25–30 years, so the roof substrate should not require replacement imminently.  
   • Load‐bearing capacity – commission a structural engineer to confirm that the roof (or supporting structure) can handle the weight of rails, panels and wind/snow loads.  
   • Orientation, tilt‐angle and shading analysis – evaluate annual solar yield based on azimuth, pitch and any nearby trees or buildings that could cast shadows.

3. Technical and grid considerations  
   • Existing electrical installation – check switchgear capacity, potential need for a dedicated meter and whether internal wiring must be upgraded.  
   • Inverter location and cabling routes – plan where inverters, distribution boards and monitoring equipment will be placed for easy access and serviceability.  
   • Grid‐connection application – submit the technical data of panels/inverters to your grid operator and secure an agreed point of interconnection.

4. Financial analysis  
   • Investment cost vs. expected generation – obtain multiple quotations and compare yields, warranties and service plans.  
   • Available grants, subsidies or green certificates – investigate regional energy-efficiency programmes, ROT deductions and feed-in rates.  
   • Pay-back period and lifecycle cost – account for operating expenses, inverter replacement and potential performance degradation.

5. Procurement and contracts  
   • Installer qualifications and references – choose an installer certified under recognized schemes (e.g., SolEl-certifierat i Sverige).  
   • Performance guarantees and warranties – verify panel (25 years) and inverter (5–10 years) warranties, plus workmanship guarantees from the installer.  
   • Service and maintenance plan – agree on monitoring, cleaning and preventive maintenance arrangements.

6. Impact on building energy certificate (EPC)  
   • EPC energy class (epc_egienergiklass) – installing solar panels may improve your building’s energy performance rating. Keep your EPC updated to reflect the new installation.

By working through each of these six areas—with professional advice where needed—you’ll minimize unexpected costs or delays and ensure a compliant, cost-effective solar installation.

To reduce the energy used for domestic hot water (DHW) in an apartment building, you can pursue measures in four broad areas: production, distribution, consumption and user behavior. Below are detailed strategies in each category:

1. Optimize Hot-Water Production  
 • High-Efficiency Heat Generators  
   – Replace old boilers with condensing gas boilers or electric heat pumps sized specifically for DHW demand.  
   – Where available, connect to district heating and ensure the heat exchanger is well maintained.  
 • Solar Thermal Pre-Heating  
   – Install solar thermal collectors on the roof to pre-heat input water.  
   – Combine with the existing boiler or heat pump in a cascade configuration so that the renewable source carries the base load.  
 • Heat Recovery from Greywater  
   – Implement plate or rotary heat exchangers on wastewater from showers/baths to capture up to 50 % of the heat before it goes down the drain.  
   – Consider building-integrated systems that recover heat from other building ventilation streams.

2. Improve Distribution Efficiency  
 • Pipe Insulation and Routing  
   – Insulate all DHW pipes and storage tanks to minimize conductive and convective losses.  
   – Shorten distribution loops and avoid oversizing – smaller diameter and shorter runs deliver hot water faster and with less standing loss.  
 • Central vs. Decentral Systems  
   – If you have a central hot-water tank, locate it as close as possible to high-demand cores (e.g., kitchens and bathrooms).  
   – In larger buildings, consider distributed mini-boilers or point-of-use heat pumps in risers to reduce recirculation needs.

3. Reduce End-Use Consumption  
 • Low-Flow Fixtures and Aerators  
   – Fit showers, faucets and taps with low-flow aerators (flow rates down to 6 L/min) and pressure regulators.  
 • Thermostatic Mixing and Temperature Control  
   – Install thermostatic mixing valves to ensure a stable outlet temperature (e.g., 50 °C) and avoid overheating.  
   – Lower the set-point on the storage tank to the minimum safe level (typically 60 °C for Legionella protection).  

4. Monitor, Control and Engage Users  
 • Sub-Metering and Remote Monitoring  
   – Install apartment-level DHW meters to encourage conservation and allow for tenant billing by actual use.  
   – Use data logging to identify abnormal consumption (leaks, faulty fixtures).  
 • Smart Control Systems  
   – Implement time-of-use or demand-controlled circulation pumps that only run when there is demand.  
   – Use building automation to adjust pump speeds, storage temperatures and charging schedules to off-peak electricity or heat prices.  
 • Resident Education  
   – Share clear guidance on best practices (e.g., shorter showers, reporting leaks promptly).  
   – Provide feedback on monthly consumption to foster awareness and behavioural change.

Maintenance and Regular Commissioning  
 • Descale and clean heat exchangers, tank elements and filters to maintain optimal performance.  
 • Check insulation, valves, pump operation and sensor calibration at least annually.

By combining high-efficiency generation, well-insulated distribution, low-flow fixtures, smart controls and user engagement, an apartment building can typically reduce its DHW energy demand by 30–50 %. Implementing these measures will not only lower operating costs but also improve the building’s overall energy performance and EPC rating.

Ventilation balancing is the process of measuring and adjusting the airflows in a mechanical ventilation system so that each supply and exhaust outlet actually delivers (or removes) the designed volume of air.  In practice this means:

• Measuring the actual airflow (e.g. in l/s or m³/h) at each supply grille and exhaust register.  
• Adjusting fan speeds, dampers or diffusers so that each zone of the building gets exactly the air change rate it was designed for.  
• Ensuring that overall supply and exhaust volumes match (or nearly match) so the building is neither overly pressurised nor depressurised.

Why it matters for energy use  
1. Minimises uncontrolled heat loss or gain – If you’re over-ventilating, you’re letting conditioned (heated or cooled) air escape, and drawing in outdoor air that must be reheated or recooled.  
2. Optimises heat‐recovery performance – In balanced systems with heat‐recovery units, equal supply and extract flows through the exchanger maximise heat transfer, recovering up to 70–90 % of the energy that would otherwise be lost.  
3. Reduces fan energy – When fans and dampers are set to their design points, the system runs more efficiently and avoids the extra electrical consumption of oversized flows.  
4. Improves indoor comfort and air quality – Properly balanced airflow prevents drafts, hot or cold spots and humidity issues, reducing the need for supplemental heating, cooling or dehumidification.

In short, a well-balanced ventilation installation delivers the right amount of fresh air where it’s needed, recovers as much waste heat as possible and keeps both heating/cooling and fan-power demand to a minimum.

Yes. Lowering your indoor temperature is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to reduce heating energy use. Here’s why—and how much you can expect to save:

1. Heat-loss principle  
   - Every degree you lower your thermostat set-point reduces the temperature difference (ΔT) between inside and outside.  
   - Since heat‐loss through walls, windows and the roof is roughly proportional to ΔT, a lower set-point directly cuts your heat losses.

2. Rule of thumb for savings  
   - A common estimate is that reducing the indoor temperature by 1 °C saves about 5 % of your annual heating energy.  
   - For example, if you normally keep your home at 21 °C and lower it to 19 °C, you could save roughly 10 % on your heating bill.

3. Practical recommendations  
   - Daytime set-point: 19–20 °C for living areas.  
   - Nighttime or unoccupied rooms: 16–18 °C.  
   - Use a programmable or smart thermostat to automatically adjust temperatures when you sleep or are away.  

4. Comfort and health considerations  
   - Dropping below 16 °C for extended periods can lead to discomfort, poor sleep or mould risk in poorly insulated buildings.  
   - Strike a balance—small temperature setbacks (1–2 °C) are usually well tolerated and still yield significant savings.

5. Combine with other measures  
   - Improve insulation, seal drafts and optimize ventilation to multiply your savings.  
   - Regularly maintain your heating system (e.g., bleed radiators, clean filters).

In summary, lowering the indoor temperature by just a degree or two is a very effective energy‐saving measure—simple to implement, no capital cost, and typically paying back in a matter of weeks or months.

When funds are tight, the board’s goal is to get the biggest “bang for the krona” by tackling measures with the highest energy‐savings per cost and shortest pay-back time first. A typical five-step approach looks like this:

1. Secure an energy overview  
   • Order a targeted energy audit (or consult your most recent Energy Performance Certificate – EPC) to identify where heat and electricity are lost most.  
   • Map out both building-wide systems (heating, ventilation, lighting) and the building envelope (walls, windows, roof).

2. Identify and implement “no-regret” measures  
   • Adjust and optimize controls: thermostat set-points, radiator balancing, ventilations schedules.  
   • Upgrade to LED lighting in common areas and boiler rooms.  
   • Seal obvious air leaks around doors, windows and service penetrations.

3. Tackle quick-pay-back retrofits  
   • Improve attic or roof insulation, where accessible, since loose-fill or batt insulation is relatively low cost.  
   • Install draft strips or tighter glazing seals on windows.  
   • Add simple heat-recovery units in laundry or drying rooms if the audit flags excessive ventilation losses.

4. Plan medium- and long-term renovations  
   • Once cash flow allows, phase in façade insulation or exterior wall retrofits, which deliver bigger savings but require more capital.  
   • Schedule window replacements or upgrades in bundles (e.g. 10–20% of the building each year) to spread cost.  
   • Consider upgrading to a modern, high-efficiency boiler or heat‐pump system when your existing plant nears end of life.

5. Leverage financing and subsidies  
   • Apply for national or municipal grants, “gröna lån” (green loans) or tax deductions available for energy-saving measures.  
   • Explore partnering with an energy‐service company (ESCO) that can carry up-front costs in return for sharing savings.  
   • Build a renovation fund in your annual budget so you’re ready for the next phase.

By focusing first on low-cost, high-impact actions and then rolling out larger upgrades in stages—while tapping every available grant or green loan—you ensure steady progress toward a more energy-efficient, sustainable BRF without over-stretching your budget.
